References / Textile / 289

Op-art paper dress

A disposable dress of bonded-fibre paper from the Scott Paper Company, printed all over with a black and white op-art check.

Source
V&A: Dress, T.30-1992
Creator
Scott Paper Company (maker)
Made
1966
Style
Op art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Vibrating, mod, disposable
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.30-1992 (1200 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A catalogues the dress with the style “Op art” and describes “a repeating black and white op art printed pattern” on bonded fibre paper. V&A.

The V&A says Scott Paper Company invented the paper dress in 1966 as a marketing tool: for one dollar a buyer got the dress and coupons for Scott paper products, and the company received about half a million orders in under a year. V&A.

A later promotional paper dress with a Pop print is the Campbell’s “Souper” dress.

Observed

  • A sleeveless A-line shift with a round neck and two patch pockets, photographed flat on black.
  • The whole surface carries one black and white print: checkerboard bands in which the squares change size, alternating with rows of small open squares inside larger ones.
  • Where fine checks meet coarse checks, the rows seem to bend and bulge.
  • The print runs across the seams and pockets without matching them. A plain white band finishes the hem.

Why it belongs

The dress applies the op rule of one unit changed by steps: the square is the only motif, and only its size and grouping change.

As a throwaway paper product, it shows how quickly the gallery look of 1965 became a mass-market print.

Borrow

Build a pattern from one square unit whose size changes by steps across bands.

Let an all-over pattern run through seams, pockets, or panel edges, so that the field reads as continuous.
